7:2.text: And if a kingdom be divided against itself, that kingdom cannot stand.

provenance.other: “house be divided” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:25, and “cannot stand” in exactly four, of which three are Mark 3:24, 3:25 and 3:26. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, “divided one against another”, reproduces neither, and “one against another” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses, none of them the Synoptic saying. The link therefore rests on the idiom and its consequence, not on a run of words — which is why it is filed as an echo.
provenance.significance: The saying withholds the outcome — a divided kingdom 'cannot stand' — and 3 Nephi 7:2 supplies it in the same sentence: 'thus they did destroy the government of the land.' What is worth recording is not this verse alone but where it sits. Mark 3 is the chapter behind 7:16's eight-word run, and the material 3 Nephi 7 takes from it arrives in Mark's own order of concerns: the division that cannot stand (3:24-26) at 7:2, Satan as the agent of it (3:23, 3:26) at 7:5, the prophet grieved at the hardness of their hearts (3:5) at 7:16, and unclean spirits cast out by a delegated power (3:11, 3:15) at 7:19. Read alone this row is thin; read as the first stop on that route it is part of the chapter's principal finding.

7:2.note: 'And the people were divided one against another; and they did separate one from another, into tribes … and thus they did destroy the government of the land.' The Synoptic division saying is the King James Bible's one formulation of the idea that internal division destroys a polity, and this is the sentence in which the Nephite polity is destroyed by internal division. The Book of Mormon has already used the idiom at Helaman 10:18 in a reflexive plural that matches no single verse; 3 Nephi is a new book and a new narrator, so the row is written again here rather than cross-referenced (ADJUDICATING §4). Note that the division here runs along exactly the lines Luke 12:52-53 makes the mark of the kingdom's arrival — family, kindred, friends — but inverted: there the household divides, here the household is the unit that survives and the nation dissolves around it.
7:2.whyNot: No distinctive wording is reproduced. A reader who wants the connection has to accept that 'divided one against another' is reaching for 'divided against itself', and it may simply be the ordinary English way of saying what happened.

7:8.text: But it is happened unto them according to the true proverb, The dog is turned to his own vomit again; and the sow that was washed to her wallowing in the mire.

provenance.route: Proverbs 26:11 → 2 Peter 2:22 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “wallowing in the mire” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Peter 2:22, and so does “the sow that was washed”. The other half of the couplet is the Proverbs form: “to his vomit” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Proverbs 26:11, and 2 Peter reads 'to his own vomit again'. So the Book of Mormon's dog is Solomon's and its sow is Peter's.
provenance.alternative: Proverbs 26:11 alone. It is ruled out by the sow, which is in no Old Testament verse; the swine half of the proverb enters the Bible only at 2 Peter 2:22, where it is paired with a non-canonical saying.
provenance.significance: Recover 2 Peter 2:20-22 and the borrowing acquires its clock. Peter's proverb is applied to people who 'have escaped the pollutions of the world through the knowledge of the Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ' and 'are again entangled therein', for whom 'the latter end is worse with them than the beginning' — apostasy after knowledge, not sin in ignorance. That is precisely the arithmetic 3 Nephi 7:8 is making: 'thus six years had not passed away, since the more part of the people had turned from their righteousness', six years measured from the signs of Christ's birth in 3 Nephi 1. And 2 Peter 2:21's definition of the offence — 'after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them' — is restated seven verses later at 7:15 as their 'quick return from righteousness unto their wickedness and abominations'. The epistle is not being quoted for a picturesque image; it is supplying the category the chapter needs.

7:8.note: 'The more part of the people had turned from their righteousness, like the dog to his vomit, or like the sow to her wallowing in the mire.' Both animals, in Peter's order, with the mire clause reproduced word for word. This falls well below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and is not one of his thirty-six, but the mediation is not in doubt: 2 Peter 2:22 is the only verse in the Bible that has the sow, and the run “to her wallowing in the mire” is its alone. What the Book of Mormon does not take is Peter's 'own' and his 'again' — 'like the dog to his vomit' is the Proverbs wording, so the verse is a composite rather than a straight lift, and the mediation-check divides three decisive points to one on that account.

7:10.text: Which thing I also did in Jerusalem: and many of the saints did I shut up in prison, having received authority from the chief priests; and when they were put to death, I gave my voice against them.

provenance.other: “gave my voice against” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 26:10; “voice against” occurs in exactly two, the other being Jeremiah 4:16, where it is a herald's shout at Jerusalem and not a vote. The idiom is also distinctively King James: the Greek is a ballot cast, and modern versions read 'cast my vote against them', which removes the voice entirely. A reader of any twentieth-century Bible cannot find this phrase.
provenance.significance: Paul's sentence is a confession of judicial murder made to Agrippa — he is describing, as the chief of persecutors, his own consent to the killing of the saints, and Acts 7:58 has already shown him holding the clothes at the stoning of a witness. 3 Nephi 7:10 gives that sentence to the man the secret combination has just crowned: 'he was one of the chiefest which had given his voice against the prophets which testified of Jesus.' The metalepsis works in both directions. It makes Jacob the Nephite Saul of Tarsus, formally casting his vote for the deaths of those who testify of Jesus; and it silently withholds what makes Paul's sentence bearable in Acts, which is that the speaker has since been converted and is telling the story against himself. Jacob is made king instead. Note also that the stoning of prophets Acts 7:58 attaches to Saul turns up four verses later at 7:14.

7:10.note: 'And he was one of the chiefest which had given his voice against the prophets which testified of Jesus.' The KJV has exactly one verse in which a man gives his voice against people who are put to death, and it is Paul's account of his own part in the executions at Jerusalem. The Book of Mormon takes the idiom whole and keeps its legal sense — a formal assent to a death sentence, not mere speech against — which is why the verse can call Jacob 'one of the chiefest' of a body rather than a lone accuser. Whether 'chiefest' is also reaching for Paul's 'very chiefest apostles' is not decidable: “chiefest” occurs in exactly eight KJV verses across both testaments, and the word is not rare enough to carry the weight.

7:15.text: For we have not followed cunningly devised fables, when we made known unto you the power and coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, but were eyewitnesses of his majesty.

provenance.other: “eyewitnesses” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Luke 1:2 and 2 Peter 1:16, and the word occurs nowhere else in the Bible in any form. The 1830 reading is the singular 'eyewitness', twice, which 1920 hyphenated to 'eye-witness'; neither spelling is in the KJV, but the noun itself is confined to those two verses.
provenance.alternative: Luke 1:2, 'which from the beginning were eyewitnesses, and ministers of the word' — attractive because 3 Nephi 7:15-17 pairs eyewitness with ministry twice ('the ministry of Christ', 'he did minister many things'). It is not preferred because Luke's eyewitnesses are other people, cited by a writer who was not one, whereas 2 Peter's are the writer himself, which is Nephi's position here.
provenance.significance: 2 Peter 1:16-18 is the KJV's one first-person claim to have both seen and heard: 'we were eyewitnesses of his majesty … And this voice which came from heaven we heard, when we were with him in the holy mount.' 3 Nephi 7:15 builds its credential the same way and in the same order — visited by angels, and also by the voice of the Lord, therefore having seen angels, and being eyewitness. What makes the route worth naming is that the chapter has already been to this epistle: 7:8 takes the dog and the sow from 2 Peter 2:22, and 2 Peter 2:21's 'after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment' is what 7:15 calls their 'quick return from righteousness unto their wickedness'. Two contacts with a three-chapter epistle in eight verses, and both fall in the part of it that is about apostasy after knowledge.

7:15.note: 'Nephi, having been visited by angels, and also by the voice of the Lord, therefore having seen angels, and being eyewitness.' The word 'eyewitness' is not ordinary English scripture vocabulary — it is in two verses of the Bible and no more — and the sentence that carries it here reproduces 2 Peter's structure of a voice heard and a glory seen. The link is conceptual rather than verbal because no clause is shared; what is shared is a rare noun and the shape of the claim it underwrites.
7:15.whyNot: A single rare word plus a structural resemblance. Luke 1:2 has the same word and the ministry vocabulary that surrounds it here, and a reader could reasonably prefer that verse or decline both.

7:16.text: And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand. And he stretched it out: and his hand was restored whole as the other.

provenance.other: “being grieved for the hardness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and so does “hardness of their hearts”; both are Mark 3:5. Check the pronoun before assuming it: “hardness of your hearts” occurs in exactly one KJV verse and it is Matthew 19:8, on divorce, which is not this verse. The Book of Mormon has the third person, and therefore Mark.
provenance.significance: The catalogue has recorded this clause nine times before, so what earns a fresh argument here is not the phrase but what the chapter does with the rest of Mark 3. Mark 3:5 is not a lament, it is a hinge: Jesus, grieved at the hardness of their hearts, works a healing, and the healing is what makes his opponents 'take counsel … how they might destroy him' (3:6). 3 Nephi 7:16-20 runs that hinge exactly — grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he goes forth and ministers, he casts out devils and raises the dead, 'and the people saw it … and were angry with him, because of his power.' Miracle producing murderous anger is the Markan sequence and it is not the obvious one; grief usually precedes rebuke, not wonders. And the surrounding chapter keeps returning to the same page of Mark: the divided house that cannot stand (3:24-26) at 7:2, Satan as its agent (3:23) at 7:5, unclean spirits and a delegated power to cast them out (3:11, 3:15) at 7:19. 3 Nephi 7 is the Book of Mormon's most sustained single-chapter engagement with Mark 3, and this verse is the anchor that keeps the rest from being coincidence.

7:16.note: 'Therefore, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds, went forth among them in that same year, and began to testify boldly.' Eight words of Mark 3:5 in order and unaltered, from a verse that is the sole KJV home of both of its distinctive phrases. Below Skousen's sixteen-word threshold and not one of his thirty-six, but dependence here is not seriously deniable. The clause is by now a Book of Mormon formula — it has appeared in five previous books — and per ADJUDICATING §4 the row is written again because 3 Nephi is a new book and a new hand; the argument for the borrowing itself was made at 1 Nephi 2:18 and is not restated. What is new is the context: this is the first time a Book of Mormon narrator uses it of himself in the situation Mark 3 gives it, a prophet grieved and then attacked for the miracle that follows.

7:16.text: And that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem.

provenance.other: “repentance and remission of sins” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Luke 24:47. The looser “remission of sins” occurs in exactly seven, and the near neighbours — Mark 1:4 and Luke 3:3, 'the baptism of repentance for the remission of sins' — put the two nouns in a different relation. Only Luke 24:47 conjoins them.
provenance.significance: Luke 24:47 is the risen Christ's last commission, three verses before the ascension: repentance and remission of sins 'preached in his name among all nations, beginning at Jerusalem'. 3 Nephi 7 puts that commission into effect in the thirty-first year, and the rest of it turns up in the neighbouring verses — 'in his name' at 7:19-20, 'in the name of Jesus', and 'among all nations' as the whole premise of a book claiming the commission reached a people outside Jerusalem. The chronology is the finding. In Luke the words are spoken by the risen Lord and then obeyed; here they are obeyed at 7:16 and 7:23 and the risen Lord does not arrive to speak them until 3 Nephi 11. The preaching precedes the commission that authorises it, which is the Book of Mormon's characteristic anachronism stated as compactly as anywhere in the book.

7:16.note: 'Began to testify boldly, repentance and remission of sins through faith on the Lord Jesus Christ.' Five words of a KJV singleton, and the whole content of Nephi's preaching for the next eight verses: 7:23 repeats the phrase exactly ('he did preach unto them repentance and remission of sins') and 7:25 completes it with 'received a remission of their sins'. Because both occurrences fall in one chapter the borrowing is adjudicated here at first use and 7:23 is recorded in recurrenceRefs. Note that the KJV's own commonest form of the phrase is Mark 1:4's, which subordinates remission to baptism; the Book of Mormon has Luke's coordinate pair, and then supplies the baptism separately at 7:24-25.

7:16.text: Having the understanding darkened, being alienated from the life of God through the ignorance that is in them, because of the blindness of their heart:

provenance.route: Ephesians 4:18 + 2 Corinthians 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “blindness of their minds” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses. Both of its halves are KJV singletons of different verses: “blindness of their heart” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Ephesians 4:18, and the blinding of minds is 2 Corinthians 4:4, 'the god of this world hath blinded the minds of them which believe not'.
provenance.significance: The phrase is a fusion, and the two verses fused are the New Testament's two accounts of why unbelievers cannot see — Ephesians 4:18's self-inflicted hardening and 2 Corinthians 4:4's blinding by the god of this world. 3 Nephi 7 has already said which of the two it means: at 7:5 'they did yield themselves unto the power of satan', which is 2 Corinthians 4:4's mechanism and not Ephesians'. So the composite is not careless; the minds come from the verse where an external power blinds them and the blindness comes from the verse where the fault is their own, and the chapter has narrated both.

7:16.note: 'Being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, and the blindness of their minds.' The pair of clauses is what makes this worth a row: the first is Mark 3:5 unaltered, and the second is a phrase that exists in no King James verse but is assembled out of two that do. Ephesians 4:18 supplies 'blindness of their —' and 2 Corinthians 4:4 supplies the organ, its 'blinded the minds of them which believe not' standing four words from the dossier's independently-ranked match at 7:14. Recorded as an echo because neither source is reproduced intact; recorded at all because a hybrid of two singletons is better evidence of reading than either singleton alone would be.
7:16.whyNot: Hearts and minds are an easy English doublet, and a writer who had just written 'hardness of their hearts' might reach for 'blindness of their minds' without any verse behind it. The case rests on the arithmetic of the two singletons, not on any run of words.

7:17.text: And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of his disciples, which are not written in this book:

provenance.route: John 20:30-31 and 21:25 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “not written in this book” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 20:30. The bare “written in this book” occurs in exactly twelve, mostly Deuteronomic curse formulae, so the negative is what identifies the source. The second half of the Book of Mormon's sentence answers to John 21:25, whose hyperbole is that 'even the world itself could not contain the books that should be written'.
provenance.significance: John's two colophons do different work — 20:30-31 says the record is a selection made so that the reader may believe, 21:25 says the whole could not be written at all — and 3 Nephi 7:17 uses both in one sentence: 'all of them cannot be written, and a part of them would not suffice; therefore they are not written in this book.' What the borrowing does is transfer the evangelist's sign-off to a prophet. In John the unwritten signs are Jesus's; here they are Nephi's, and the next verse explains why the substitution is not presumptuous — 'so great was his faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, that angels did minister unto him daily'. Recover John 20:31 and the borrowed clause carries its purpose clause with it: 'but these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus is the Christ.' 3 Nephi 7:21 states the same result four verses on, of those 'which was in Jesus Christ, in whom they believed'.

7:17.note: 'And all of them cannot be written, and a part of them would not suffice; therefore they are not written in this book.' Six words of a KJV singleton, in order and unchanged. The catalogue has adjudicated the same formula at Mosiah 1:8 and Alma 13:31 and it is written again here because 3 Nephi is a new book (ADJUDICATING §4); what is new in this occurrence is that it is applied to signs and miracles rather than to words, which is John 20:30's own referent and not Mosiah's or Alma's. “many other signs” also occurs in exactly one KJV verse, the same one, which is worth noticing given that 7:22 goes on to say the converts 'did shew forth signs also'.

7:18.text: And he was there in the wilderness forty days, tempted of Satan; and was with the wild beasts; and the angels ministered unto him.

provenance.other: “angels ministered unto him” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 1:13. The only other angelic ministration in the KJV is Matthew 4:11, “angels came and ministered”, which also occurs in exactly one verse; both are the close of the temptation.
provenance.significance: In the King James Bible there is exactly one man to whom angels minister, and the ministration is what follows his refusal of Satan. 3 Nephi 7 has set that refusal up as the chapter's governing contrast: at 7:5 the people 'did yield themselves unto the power of satan', and at 7:18 the one man who did not is served by angels daily. The Book of Mormon has taken a phrase the gospels use once, at the end of forty days in the wilderness, and made it a standing condition — 'daily' is its own word and it is the word that converts an episode into a station. Note also what the borrowing costs the sentence: the phrase's home context makes the angelic ministry a consolation after temptation, and here it is the explanation of why a prophet's enemies cannot answer him.

7:18.note: 'For so great was his faith on the Lord Jesus Christ, that angels did minister unto him daily.' Four words of a KJV singleton with the auxiliary changed and 'daily' added. The rarity is absolute — the KJV gives an angelic ministration to nobody but Jesus, and gives it twice in one episode — so the claim being made about Nephi is precise and is made by the choice of phrase rather than by any assertion.
7:18.whyNot: Short, and the words are ordinary; a writer describing angels serving a man has few other ways to say it. The row rests on the fact that the KJV, having many angels, uses this construction for one man only.

7:19.text: And these signs shall follow them that believe; In my name shall they cast out devils; they shall speak with new tongues;

provenance.other: “in the name of Jesus” occurs in exactly six KJV verses and “cast out devils” in exactly twelve, so neither identifies a source alone; what narrows it is the pairing of the name with the casting out, which is Mark 16:17's 'In my name shall they cast out devils'. Two further phrases are singletons: “signs following” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 16:20, against 7:22's 'they did shew forth signs also', and “power to heal sicknesses” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Mark 3:15, against 7:18-19's 'he had greater power … did he cast out devils'. “devils and unclean spirits” occurs in exactly zero KJV verses; Mark 3 has the two terms in one chapter, at 3:11 and 3:15.
provenance.significance: Mark 16:17-20 is the KJV's list of what believers will do after the ascension, and the point of the list is that the works are delegated: they are done 'in my name', by people who are not Jesus, with the Lord 'working with them, and confirming the word with signs following'. 3 Nephi 7:19-22 is that list executed — devils cast out in the name of Jesus, the dead raised, miracles done in the sight of the people, and the healed themselves showing forth signs. The chronological point is the same one Luke 24:47 makes at 7:16, and sharper: the longer ending of Mark describes the church's life after the resurrection, and here it is being lived four chapters before the resurrected Christ arrives. Mark 3:15 supplies the same commission in its pre-resurrection form — power to heal sicknesses and to cast out devils, given to men who are ordained — and 7:25 will ordain them.

7:19.note: 'And in the name of Jesus did he cast out devils and unclean spirits; and even his brother did he raise from the dead.' No clause is reproduced, which is why the row is conceptual, but the inventory is Mark's and so is its governing formula: works done by a man in the name of Jesus. The verses that follow keep to the list — miracles in the sight of the people (7:20), devils cast out and infirmities healed (7:22), signs shewn forth (7:22, where the 1830's 'shew' preserves the KJV spelling that 1920 modernised). Both later verses are recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given rows of their own, since they are the same borrowing continuing.
7:19.whyNot: The vocabulary of casting out devils is common enough in the gospels that no single verse is demonstrable, and a case could be made for Matthew 10:1 or Mark 3:15 instead of the longer ending. The row claims the passage is working from Mark's signs-list, not that it is quoting one verse of it.

7:24.text: For John truly baptized with water; but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence.

provenance.other: “baptized with water” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Acts 1:5 and Acts 11:16, and the second is Peter quoting the first. John 1:26 and 1:31 have 'baptize with water' and 'baptizing with water', not the past participle. So the Book of Mormon's phrase is, in the KJV, one saying of the risen Lord and its later citation.
provenance.significance: The phrase is never neutral in the KJV. Both times it appears it is the first half of a contrast whose second half is the whole point — 'but ye shall be baptized with the Holy Ghost not many days hence' — and at Acts 1:5 the not-many-days is ten, until Pentecost. 3 Nephi 7:24-26 is emphatic that the baptism it is describing is with water and says nothing about the Holy Ghost; the reader is at the close of the thirty-third year, and 3 Nephi 9:20 will promise 'baptize with fire and with the Holy Ghost', 3 Nephi 11 will bring the risen Christ, and 3 Nephi 19:13 will deliver the fire. The suppressed half of Acts 1:5 is the Book of Mormon's next four chapters. Mormon's editorial aside — 'Now I would have you to remember also' — is asking the reader to hold exactly the thing Acts 1:5 makes provisional.

7:24.note: 'Now I would have you to remember also, that there were none which were brought unto repentance, who were not baptized with water.' The insistence on water, twice in two verses, is the point of the passage, and 'baptized with water' in that participial form is a two-verse phrase in the KJV, both of them Acts 1:5's saying. What is being remembered is a limit: this was water only. 7:25 repeats the phrase and is recorded in recurrenceRefs rather than given its own row for it.

7:25.text: Beginning from the baptism of John, unto that same day that he was taken up from us, must one be ordained to be a witness with us of his resurrection.

provenance.other: “ordained to be a witness” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Acts 1:22. “were ordained” occurs in exactly two, Acts 13:48 and 16:4, neither of which is an ordination to office. The Book of Mormon's own phrase, 'ordained of Nephi, men unto this ministry … as a witness and a testimony', separates the two words that Acts 1:22 joins but keeps both.
provenance.significance: Acts 1:21-22 is the KJV's one description of what a man is ordained for, and the answer is: to be a witness of the resurrection. The requirement is retrospective — the candidate must have companied with the apostles from the baptism of John — and the office is filled before Pentecost, in the ten-day gap. 3 Nephi 7:25 ordains men in the same gap and to the same office, and the resurrection they are ordained to witness has not happened yet. Read with 7:24's Acts 1:5, the whole passage sits inside Acts 1: baptism with water at 7:24, ordination to be a witness at 7:25, and the Holy Ghost withheld until the Lord comes. These are the men Christ will call at 3 Nephi 11-12, and the Book of Mormon has already given them Matthias's job description.

7:25.note: 'Therefore there were ordained of Nephi, men unto this ministry … and this as a witness and a testimony before God, and unto the people.' Ordination plus witness is a rare conjunction in the KJV — one verse — and it belongs to the appointment of Matthias, the one apostolic ordination the New Testament narrates. Mark 3:14's 'he ordained twelve' is the alternative and is not preferred, because the Book of Mormon supplies the witness language that Mark's verse lacks and Acts 1:22 has.
7:25.whyNot: The shared words are 'ordained' and 'witness', both ordinary, and the Book of Mormon's sentence is about baptism rather than about apostleship. The case is that the KJV joins these two words once, and that 7:24 has already put the passage in Acts 1.
